definition: Artificial grammar learning (AGL) is a paradigm of study within cognitive psychology and linguistics.
details: Its goal is to investigate the processes that underlie human language learning by testing subjects' ability to learn a made-up grammar in a laboratory setting. It was developed to evaluate the processes of human language learning but has also been utilized to study implicit learning in a more general sense. The area of interest is typically the subjects' ability to detect patterns and statistical regularities during a training phase and then use their new knowledge of those patterns in a testing phase. The testing phase can either use the symbols or sounds used in the training phase or transfer the patterns to another set of symbols or sounds as surface structure. Many researchers propose that the rules of the artificial grammar are learned on an implicit level since the rules of the grammar are never explicitly presented to the participants. The paradigm has also recently been utilized for other areas of research such as language learning aptitude, structural priming and to investigate which brain structures are involved in syntax acquisition and implicit learning. Apart from humans, the paradigm has also been used to investigate pattern learning in other species, e.g. cottontop tamarins and starlings.

explainer.lead: Artificial grammar learning is a laboratory method for studying how people pick up patterns without being taught the rules directly. By simplifying language-like learning to made-up symbols or sounds, it helps researchers examine pattern detection, implicit learning, and aspects of language acquisition.

tiers.eli5: Imagine hearing several made-up songs that all follow the same hidden pattern, without anyone explaining it. Later, you are asked which new songs sound as though they belong. Artificial grammar learning uses a similar game to study how you noticed and reused the pattern.
tiers.practitioner: A typical study exposes participants to sequences generated by an artificial grammar, then tests their responses to new grammatical and ungrammatical sequences. A transfer condition can replace the training symbols or sounds while preserving the underlying pattern. When designing or interpreting a study, keep training exposure separate from test performance, and do not treat successful classification alone as proof of a particular learning mechanism.
tiers.paperLevel: Let G be a made-up grammar over symbols or sounds: participants receive training sequences generated according to G, then are tested on their ability to use the acquired regularities, sometimes after a change of surface alphabet. A minimal worked form is train = {AB, ABB, ABBB}, with test items such as ABBBB and BA. AGL was developed for human language-learning research and is also used to study implicit learning more generally; the sources characterize implicit rule learning as a proposal by many researchers, not a settled conclusion.

explainer.example: Suppose the hidden grammar allows A followed by one or more Bs. Participants see AB, ABB, and ABBB during training; at test time, ABBBB follows the pattern while BA does not, and XYYY can test transfer of the same pattern to new symbols.

explainer.intuition: If people can learn a small invented pattern in a controlled setting, researchers can study the learning process without the full complexity of a natural language. The central question is whether exposure during training lets participants recognize or reuse regularities during testing.
howItWorks: Create a grammar that determines which sequences of symbols or sounds follow its pattern.
During training, present participants with sequences that follow the grammar without explicitly stating its rules.
During testing, present new sequences and assess whether participants use the patterns they encountered.
Optionally change the surface symbols or sounds while retaining the underlying pattern to test transfer.
Use test performance to investigate pattern learning and, with appropriate caution, possible implicit learning.
explainer.whyItMatters: AGL provides a controlled way to study how regularities are acquired and transferred, connecting research on language learning with broader questions about implicit learning. Its use with humans and other species also allows pattern learning to be investigated beyond human language.
misconceptions: Participants are not explicitly taught the artificial grammar's rules during the standard paradigm.
AGL is not limited to human language research; it is also used to study general implicit learning and pattern learning in other species.
Successful test performance does not, by itself, establish that the grammar was learned implicitly.
